svg.text: The grid walk — why a cluster’s CTAs land contiguously
The KMU walks the grid two levels deep. The inner level fills a cluster before the outer level moves on, so a cluster’s K CTAs are consecutive in dispatch order.
grid_dim = (6, 4, 1) cluster_dim = (2, 2, 1) → 24 CTAs in 6 clusters of 4
Cell number = dispatch order. Cell subscript = block_idx. Purple = is_first_of_cluster.
A flat row-major walk would emit 0,1,2,3,4,5 across the top row — the four members of a cluster would be scattered across the grid and could not co-reside.
block_idx[i] = group_origin[i] + intra_offset[i]
intra_offset advances by 1 and wraps at cluster_dim[i]; when it fully wraps, group_origin advances by cluster_dim[i].
block_idx X →
Inner level — fill the cluster
intra_x_wrap = (intra_x_n == cluster_dim[0])
intra_y_wrap = intra_x_wrap && (...)
Bounded by NUM_WARPS (members co-reside on one
core), so NW_WIDTH+1 bits — not a 32-bit counter.
Outer level — move to the next cluster
group_complete = intra_z_wrap
origin_x_n = group_origin[0] + cluster_dim[0]
Advances in (X, Y, Z) order against grid_dim.
cluster_dim = (1,1,1) is the degenerate case
Every intra_offset wraps immediately, so group_origin
advances every beat and block_idx is the plain
row-major walk. This is the default.
is_first_of_cluster is a REGISTER
reg is_first_r;
is_first_r <= group_complete;
Not the combinational predicate intra_offset == 0.
The next fire starts a cluster exactly when this one
completes one, so the walk tracks it in lockstep.
Every output field is flop-driven — deliberately
block_idx_r and is_first_r are registered walk variables updated alongside the counters; the rest are config or walk flops. The KMU’s output
is a chip-spanning broadcast to every core’s dispatcher, so it carries no combinational logic on the source side and adds no latency. The
32-bit block_idx add stays an internal reg→reg path (one add per axis), off both the output and the KMU→core route.
cluster_size and aligned_lmem_size are computed once per kernel and registered the same way — DCRs settle before `start`.
The programming surface — DCRs, written before `start`
The host writes these through the command processor’s DCR_WRITE path; VX_kmu latches them and never reads them back.
STARTUP_ADDR0/1 0x010 program image PC
KERNEL_ENTRY0/1 0x012 kernel entry PC
STARTUP_ARG0/1 0x014 kargs pointer
BLOCK_DIM_X/Y/Z 0x016 threads per CTA axis
GRID_DIM_X/Y/Z 0x019 CTAs per grid axis
LMEM_SIZE 0x01C per-CTA LMEM bytes
BLOCK_SIZE 0x01D total threads per CTA
WARP_STEP_X/Y/Z 0x01E thread-index delta
CLUSTER_DIM_X/Y/Z 0x021 cluster shape
VX_DCR_KMU_STATE_BEGIN = 0x010
VX_DCR_KMU_STATE_END = 0x024
CLUSTER_DIM is internal-only: not a CSR, not on the bus.
WARP_STEP — the host does the division
The per-warp thread-index delta is derived on the
HOST, once, so the KMU never divides:
ws_x = NT % block[0]
ws_y = (NT / block[0]) % block[1]
ws_z = (NT / (block[0]*block[1])) % block[2]
ctx_id — the launch identity
An 8-bit counter bumped on every `start`, carried on
every CTA. It is what tells a dispatcher that a NEW
launch has begun, so relaunching the same kernel at
the same PC is still a distinct context.
Keyed on the launch id, not the PC — see the init record.
AN EMPTY GRID IS NOT A NO-OP
grid_nonempty = (grid_dim[0] != 0) && (grid_dim[1] != 0) && (grid_dim[2] != 0)
The walk’s wrap comparisons test origin_*_n == grid_dim[*], and a zero bound can never be reached — so starting the
walk on an empty grid would fire CTAs forever. `running` is armed only when the grid is non-empty.
A grid-less start is instead a DELEGATED DRAW LAUNCH: the KMU walks no CTAs and forwards the frame kick to the
raster engines over VX_raster_launch_if. raster_start_r holds `busy` from the start pulse until every engine has
acknowledged, so the launch fence always observes the frame. With no raster engines it self-completes.
busy = running | raster_start_r
What the KMU does NOT send
No cta_id. The RTL walk keeps a cta_id counter for tracing only — it never reaches the bus. A CTA’s architectural
VX_CSR_CTA_ID is the LOCAL dispatcher slot it lands in, assigned on arrival. Two CTAs on different cores routinely
share a cta_id; a kernel that needs its global identity reads block_idx instead.
SimX’s kmu_req_t does carry cta_id — a model-only field with no RTL counterpart (see the SimX section).
The dispatch-order contract, stated once
The K CTAs of a cluster are emitted back to back on the launch bus. That is the ENTIRE mechanism — there is no cluster tag, no rendezvous, and no
handshake between members. A dispatcher recognises a cluster solely by is_first_of_cluster arriving with a cluster_size > 1, reserves the whole window
on that beat, and then simply lets the next K−1 beats fall into the slots it already set aside.
Adjacency in the stream is not by itself adjacency on a core, so the bus carries the rest of the contract: a compute message is one CLUSTER, and every arb level
locks its input→output pair from a message’s first beat to its `eop`. The walk emits the members back to back; the lock delivers them to one core. `eop` here is
is_last_r, a registered down-counter — so clusters, not CTAs, are what round-robin across the machine.
